doc.title: Peter Ecklund interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Trad jazz festivals, part-time bands and the business of it
summary: He explains what organizers mean by trad jazz, the business-like part-time bands, and how such festivals pay modestly but build a following.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: We talked a little bit I think before the camera was rolling about this festival and the future of this festival, these kinds of festivals. And you had mentioned the trad jazz festival. Now the organizers of these festivals, when they say “trad jazz” can you tell us what they mean by that?

They mean organized bands, mostly not full time musicians — some of them very good, some of them not so good — that play a more organized repertory than — and maybe not with the same expertise that you get here — but that put on more of a show. And sometimes it’s a very hokey show, sometimes a good show, but those — and have a following, usually developed by playing in some local club and having a mailing list. A lot of these bands that are of part time musicians are really much more business-like than full time musicians because this is what they do when they’re not at the office, and they use the same skills. I mean marketing and mailing lists and Internet and all that. And some of them are very good and do very well.

That’s very interesting you know, like the band like The Bearcats and all those kind of local things, and so if you go to those things you’re going to see a group of people who’ve played together a lot, rehearsed—

Right. I mean a band I fill in for sometimes, the new Black Eagle Band in Boston, they’re mostly not full time musicians. And if you heard them individually you might or might not think that there was something special. But together they’ve got a real sound that’s kind of unmistakable. And they do very well. I mean I don’t know if they still do, but even though they all have jobs, that was a big part of their income. © Fiillius Jazz Archive -8-

Well when did you first become aware of these kinds of festivals, the San Diego and the L.A. Classic Festival and those kinds of things? I mean they’ve been going on since I guess the ‘70s, Dick Gibson.

Well Dick Gibson is a jazz party situation. That’s a little different. The ones with the mostly amateur bands are more like Sacramento, like that. And there are more of them on the west coast. But it’s a place to play and a place to acquire a following and like that. There’s really only one in the east that I do with my own group, it’s the one in Connecticut, and we played there with the Orphan Newsboys a few times, a group I play with with Marty Grosz.
Do you find that if you do — is it word of mouth that gets you in these things?

I guess so. I mean I really don’t know. I don’t do a great deal of promotion myself. I should be doing more, but I mean if you’re a full time musician, the trouble is these jobs, I mean especially the trad jazz festivals, they don’t really pay that well. They’re good for acquiring a following and for selling lots of CDs, but they don’t pay as well as some of the other work I do. So it’s a little hard to get motivated to find that kind of work exclusively as opposed to some of the better paying work I do.
It may actually cost you to come to one of these, the trad jazz festivals.

Well it probably wouldn’t cost me, but I might go and then get a call like to play some festival in Europe for three times as much money and have to turn it down because I’d already signed a contract here or some other place. I mean this is all not very interesting but it’s kind of the mechanics of running a small business, which is basically what being a musician is.
